name: Pokhara
tagline: Lake city under the Annapurnas, 25 minutes by air from Kathmandu
meta_description: Pokhara travel guide: Phewa Lake, Sarangkot sunrise, paragliding, caves and waterfalls, hotels, best months and how to reach from Kathmandu or India.
summary: Pokhara is Nepal's second city and its easiest holiday base: a lake town at 822 m with Machhapuchhre (6,993 m) rising 30 km to the north. Plan three nights for Phewa Lake, Sarangkot sunrise, the caves and a paragliding flight. October to March gives the clearest mountain views.
intro: Pokhara sits in a wide valley in Kaski district, 200 km west of Kathmandu by road and 25 minutes by air. The town has two faces. Lakeside, along the eastern shore of Phewa Lake, is where most visitors stay: a 3 km strip of hotels, cafes, gear shops and boat stands. The older city to the east, around Bindhyabasini temple and the Old Bazaar, is where Pokhara's Newar traders, Gurung families and civil servants live and shop.

What makes Pokhara different from any other Nepali town is the distance to the snow. Machhapuchhre, the fish-tailed peak that is closed to climbers, stands only about 30 km from the lake, and Annapurna South, Annapurna II, Lamjung Himal and on clear days Dhaulagiri and Manaslu line the horizon. From October to March the peaks show most mornings; from June to August the town receives some of the heaviest rain in Nepal and the mountains can stay hidden for weeks.

For Indian families and couples, Pokhara is the core of most Nepal itineraries, usually paired with Kathmandu and often Chitwan or Bandipur. For trekkers it is the start and finish of the Annapurna region. Three nights is enough for the classic sights; add a fourth or fifth for paragliding, a day hike to Australian Camp or the World Peace Pagoda, or simply time on the water. Our Pokhara packages are built around these patterns.

≈ 200 km · 6–8 h by road, or 25 min flight
Phewa Lake, Machhapuchhre views, paragliding, Annapurna trek starts

highlights.title: Phewa Lake and Tal Barahi
highlights.text: Phewa is Nepal's second-largest lake. Hire a painted wooden doonga from the Barahi ghat and in five minutes you reach the two-tiered Tal Barahi temple on its island. Early morning, before the wind rises, the water holds a mirror image of Machhapuchhre.

highlights.title: Sarangkot sunrise
highlights.text: A 30–45 minute drive takes you to the Sarangkot viewpoint at about 1,600 m. At first light the sun hits Dhaulagiri, Annapurna South and Machhapuchhre in turn while the lake and town are still in shadow. It is the most popular morning outing in Pokhara.

highlights.title: Davis Falls and Gupteshwor Cave
highlights.text: On the Siddhartha Highway near the airport, Phewa's outflow drops into a narrow chasm at Davis Falls (Patale Chhango). Across the road, steps lead down into Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave, a Shiva shrine with a passage that ends behind the same waterfall.

highlights.title: International Mountain Museum
highlights.text: A large, well-laid-out museum at Ratopahiro covering the 14 peaks over 8,000 m, the first ascents, mountain peoples of Nepal and climbing gear through the decades. Allow two hours. It is the best rainy-day stop in town and children enjoy the climbing wall outside.

highlights.title: Old Bazaar and Bindhyabasini
highlights.text: Pokhara's old trading quarter keeps tiled Newar houses and small shrines along the road north of Mahendrapul. Bindhyabasini temple, on a small hill above the bazaar, is the city's most important Durga shrine and is busiest on Saturdays and during Dashain.

highlights.title: Seti Gandaki gorge
highlights.text: The milky Seti river cuts a gorge through Pokhara up to 30 m deep and in places only a few metres wide. Look down from the bridge at Mahendrapul or from the Seti gorge viewpoint near the Old Bazaar to see the water rushing far below the streets.

how_to_reach.text: Buddha Air, Yeti Airlines and Shree Airlines fly Kathmandu–Pokhara many times a day; the flight takes about 25 minutes and lands at Pokhara International Airport, about 4 km east of Lakeside. Sit on the right side out of Kathmandu for the mountains. Morning flights are the most reliable; afternoon departures are more often delayed by cloud, and schedules change by season, so check current status before you travel.

The Prithvi Highway covers the 200 km from Kathmandu in 6–8 hours by private car and 7–9 hours by tourist bus, via Mugling and Damauli. Road widening between Naubise and Mugling can add delays. From the Indian border at Sonauli–Bhairahawa, the Siddhartha Highway via Butwal and Syangja reaches Pokhara in about 7–8 hours (≈ 190 km). From Chitwan the drive is 4.5–5.5 hours.

where_to_stay: Most travellers stay at Lakeside, where Hotel Barahi and Temple Tree Resort & Spa put you a short walk from the boats, restaurants and paragliding offices. Damside, at the southern end of the lake, is quieter and has the best evening reflections; Pokhara Grande sits nearby in Pardi and is the city's largest five-star hotel with a big pool. For a lake-shore garden and no traffic, Fish Tail Lodge stands on its own peninsula reached by a hand-pulled raft. Couples and luxury travellers who want silence and a long mountain panorama choose Tiger Mountain Pokhara Lodge on a ridge about 10 km east of town.
tips: Go out on Phewa before 9 am, when the water is calm and the peaks are most likely to be clear.
Book paragliding for a morning slot in October–November; afternoon thermals are stronger but cloud often builds by 1 pm.
Carry a light rain jacket even in the dry season, because Pokhara has its own weather and short showers are common.
Domestic flights from Kathmandu allow about 10 kg checked plus 5 kg hand baggage on most airlines, so pack trek gear accordingly.
Indian rupee notes of ₹100 are widely accepted at Lakeside, but carry Nepali rupees for taxis, boats and temple offerings.

experiences.title: Phewa Lake boating to Tal Barahi temple
experiences.image_query: Tal Barahi temple Phewa Lake boats
experiences.summary: A slow row across Phewa in a painted wooden boat, with a stop at the island temple of Tal Barahi. On clear mornings Machhapuchhre is reflected in the water. It is the first thing most visitors do in Pokhara and suits every age.
body: Phewa Lake covers about 5 square kilometres along the western edge of Pokhara, with forested Raniban hill on the south shore and the Sarangkot ridge to the north. The boats are flat-bottomed wooden doongas painted red, blue and yellow, run by a boat owners' cooperative with fixed hourly rates posted at the main ghats. You can hire a boat with an oarsman, or row yourself if you are confident; life jackets are provided and should be worn.

Most trips start from the Barahi ghat in central Lakeside and head straight for Tal Barahi, the two-roofed pagoda temple dedicated to the goddess Barahi on a small island. The crossing takes five to ten minutes. Devotees bring flowers, coconuts and red powder; on Saturdays and festival days there is a queue for the boat and the shrine. Spend 15–20 minutes on the island, then ask the boatman to row towards the north shore for the clearest view of the mountains.

The light is best between 6:30 and 9 am. By late morning a breeze picks up and ripples break the reflection. A longer two-hour row can take you to the foot of the World Peace Pagoda trail on the south shore, from where you climb about 45 minutes to the stupa. In the monsoon the lake is often cloudy and grey, but the boats still run unless there is a storm.

faqs.q: How much does boating on Phewa Lake cost?
faqs.a: Rates are set by the boat cooperative and posted at the ghats. Expect roughly NPR 1,000–1,500 per boat per hour with an oarsman, slightly less if you row yourself, plus a small fee for Tal Barahi. A boat seats four to six people, so families usually share one. Rates change, so check the board at the ghat before you set off.

faqs.q: Is Phewa boating safe for children and seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. The boats are broad and stable, the lake is calm in the morning and life jackets are provided for everyone, including children. Getting in and out at the island steps needs a steady hand, so seniors should let the boatman hold the boat against the jetty. Avoid going out in strong afternoon wind or during monsoon storms.

faqs.q: Can we row to the World Peace Pagoda?
faqs.a: Yes. Ask for the drop at the south shore landing below the pagoda; the row takes about 20–30 minutes from Lakeside. From there a stone trail climbs through forest for about 45 minutes to the stupa at 1,100 m. Most people walk down the other side to Damside or take a taxi back, so agree a one-way fare with the boatman.

experiences.title: Davis Falls and Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave
experiences.best_time: Sep–Nov, when the falls are full
experiences.summary: Two sights on opposite sides of the same road near the airport: a waterfall that vanishes into a slot in the rock, and a Shiva cave whose lowest chamber looks out at that waterfall from behind. Easy to combine with the Tibetan settlement and the Mountain Museum.
body: Davis Falls, known locally as Patale Chhango or the underworld waterfall, is where the stream flowing out of Phewa Lake drops into a narrow, deep cleft and disappears underground. The English name is said to come from a Swiss visitor who was swept into the chasm in 1961. A paved garden with railings runs along the edge, so you look straight down into the spray. After the monsoon, from late August to October, the volume of water is at its highest and the noise is impressive.

Across the Siddhartha Highway is Gupteshwor Mahadev Cave, one of the most visited Shiva shrines in western Nepal. A spiral staircase leads down to a chamber holding a natural stone lingam, where priests perform puja. Beyond the shrine a damp, low passage continues to a ledge where you can see Davis Falls pouring through the rock from inside the cave. This lower section can be closed in heavy monsoon flow.

Allow about 45 minutes at each site. The cave floor is wet and slippery, so wear shoes with grip rather than sandals, and carry a light jacket because it is humid. Both sites get crowded with Indian and Nepali tour groups between 10 am and 2 pm; arrive at opening time for a quieter visit. The Tashiling Tibetan settlement and its craft shops are a few minutes' walk away. Ticket counters close in the early evening.

faqs.q: Is Gupteshwor Cave suitable for elderly visitors?
faqs.a: The upper shrine is reachable for most seniors: it is a spiral staircase of around 100 steps with handrails. The lower passage to the waterfall view is low, wet and uneven and is better skipped by anyone with knee or balance problems. Take it slowly, and wear shoes with good grip because the floor stays wet all year.

faqs.q: When is the best time to see Davis Falls?
faqs.a: September to early November, just after the monsoon, when Phewa is full and a large volume of water pours into the chasm. In the dry months of March to May the flow is much smaller. During July and August the falls are at their most powerful but the site can be crowded and rainy.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside Gupteshwor Cave?
faqs.a: Photography is usually not allowed in the main shrine chamber around the Shiva lingam, and signs or staff will tell you. Photos are generally fine in the passage and at the waterfall viewpoint at the end, though the light is low and spray covers lenses quickly. Respect any instructions from the priests.

experiences.title: Ultralight flight over Pokhara and the Annapurnas
experiences.summary: A two-seat open-cockpit ultralight takes off from Pokhara's airport area and climbs over Phewa Lake, Sarangkot and the World Peace Pagoda towards the Annapurna foothills. Longer flights fly close to Machhapuchhre's lower ridges. It suits travellers who want height without a parachute.
body: Ultralight flights have operated in Pokhara since the late 1990s. The aircraft carry one pilot and one passenger, sitting in tandem in an open or semi-enclosed cockpit under a high wing, so the view is wide and unobstructed. Operators offer flights of about 15, 30, 60 and 90 minutes. The short flight loops over the lake and town; the 30-minute flight adds Sarangkot and the World Peace Pagoda; the hour-long flight heads north towards the Annapurna foothills at around 3,000–4,000 m.

Flights run in the morning from roughly October to May, when the air is stable and the mountains are clear. Cloud usually builds over the foothills by late morning, so the first slots of the day are the ones to book. During the monsoon most operators stop flying. You wear a helmet and a warm jacket, and the pilot briefs you on the headset before take-off. A camera mounted on the wing can record the flight for an extra fee.

There is a weight limit, usually around 100–110 kg per passenger, and people with heart conditions or who are pregnant should not fly. Children can fly with parental consent from about 8–10 years depending on the operator. Prices are in US dollars for foreigners, and Indian visitors are often quoted a lower rate in Nepali rupees, so ask. Weather cancellations are refunded or rebooked. Book a day or two ahead in October and November, when morning slots fill quickly.

faqs.q: How much does an ultralight flight in Pokhara cost?
faqs.a: Expect roughly US$ 100–130 for 15 minutes, US$ 180–220 for 30 minutes and US$ 330–440 for 60–90 minutes per person, including pick-up and a short briefing. Video from a wing camera costs extra. Rates for Indian and SAARC visitors are often lower and quoted in Nepali rupees. Prices change by season, so check current rates before you travel.

faqs.q: Ultralight or paragliding: which is better in Pokhara?
faqs.a: Paragliding is quieter, cheaper and lets you glide with eagles, but stays mostly over the valley. An ultralight climbs higher, covers more ground and flies towards the mountains, with an engine and a more stable feel for nervous flyers. If you want close views of Machhapuchhre, choose the 60-minute ultralight; for the floating experience, choose paragliding.

faqs.q: Do ultralight flights run in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Generally no. Most operators fly from about October to May and pause from June to September because of rain, cloud and turbulence. Even in season, flights are morning only and are cancelled when cloud covers the hills. Keep a spare morning in your Pokhara plan so a weather cancellation can be rebooked.

faqs.q: How many days are enough for Pokhara?
faqs.a: Three nights covers the main sights: Phewa Lake and Tal Barahi, Sarangkot sunrise, Davis Falls, Gupteshwor Cave, the Mountain Museum and the World Peace Pagoda. Add a fourth night for paragliding or zipline, or a fifth for a short hike to Australian Camp or a day at Begnas Lake. Families travelling by road from Kathmandu usually want at least three nights to recover from the drive.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pokhara?
faqs.a: October to December is the best period, with dry weather, 20–25 °C days and the clearest mountain views. February and March are also good, with rhododendrons on the hills, though haze can build by April. June to August is the monsoon: Pokhara is one of the wettest places in Nepal, the peaks hide and some adventure activities stop.

faqs.q: Kathmandu to Pokhara: flight or road?
faqs.a: The flight takes about 25 minutes and costs roughly US$ 90–130 one way, while the road takes 6–8 hours by car and 7–9 hours by tourist bus. Fly if your time is short or you have elderly travellers. Drive if you want to stop at Manakamana or Bandipur on the way, or are on a tight budget. Weather can delay flights in the afternoon.

faqs.q: Is Pokhara good for a honeymoon?
faqs.a: Yes. Couples get a lake-view room, a private boat on Phewa at sunrise, a candle-lit dinner at Lakeside and a sunrise at Sarangkot, all within 30 minutes of each other. For privacy, spend two nights at a hillside lodge such as Tiger Mountain Pokhara Lodge. October, November, February and March give the best weather and mountain views.

faqs.q: Can Indians visit Pokhara without a passport?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian citizens do not need a visa for Nepal and can travel with either a valid passport or a voter ID card; children under 15 can use a birth certificate or school ID with a parent. For domestic flights inside Nepal, carry the same original photo ID. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Pokhara from the Indian border?
faqs.a: From Sonauli–Bhairahawa it is about 190 km to Pokhara via Butwal, Tansen and Syangja on the Siddhartha Highway, a drive of 7–8 hours on a winding hill road. Gorakhpur railway station is about 95 km south of Sonauli. Many Indian families combine the drive with a night in Lumbini or Tansen on the way.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Pokhara in December?
faqs.a: December days are sunny and around 18–21 °C, while nights drop to 5–8 °C. Mornings start with mist over the lake that clears by about 9 am, and the mountain views are among the clearest of the year. Bring a warm jacket for the Sarangkot sunrise, where it can be close to freezing before dawn.

Not by international standards. A good 3-star Lakeside hotel costs roughly ₹3,500–6,000 a night, a lake-view 4-star ₹7,000–12,000 and the top five-star and luxury lodges ₹15,000 and up. A dinner for two at Lakeside is ₹1,200–2,500. Adventure activities are the big extra: paragliding about ₹6,500–8,500 and the zipline about ₹6,000.

faqs.q: Can I see Everest from Pokhara?
faqs.a: No. Everest is about 300 km east of Pokhara and is not visible from the valley. From Pokhara and Sarangkot you see the Annapurna range, Machhapuchhre, Dhaulagiri and on clear days Manaslu. To see Everest, take the mountain flight from Kathmandu or a helicopter tour to the Khumbu.
